To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

chronic inhibition of NO synthesis induces oxidative stress in the myocardium, which is normalized by antioxidant intervention in NO-deficient rats, and that such an antioxidant intervention specifically attenuates up-regulation of cardiomyocyte expression of IMD and RMP1 in NO-deficient myocardium in the absence of normalization of blood pressure.

chronic inhibition of nitric-oxide synthesis in rats is associated with hypertension and cardiomyocyte hypertrophic remodeling and that the latter is accompanied by up-regulation of the expression of prepro-intermedin (IMDb) and receptor-activating modifying proteins (RAMPs) 1-3, while the expression of pre-pro-adrenomedullin remains unchanged.

chronic inhibition of NO synthesis induces oxidative stress in left ventricular cardiocytes and this is associated with increased expression of AM, IM and their respective receptor components, RAMPs and calcitonin receptor-like receptor (CLR).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of cardiomyocyte hypertrophic growth and the potential for anti-oxidant interventions to prevent such growth.
the role of oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of cardiovascular diseases.
the identification and characterization of the mechanisms that regulate cardiomyocyte expression of the AM / IMD receptor components.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

antioxidant intervention in the presence of chronic nitric oxide deficiency is associated with: (i) normalization of augmented plasma levels of intermedin, (ii) normalization of augmented expression of pre-pro-intermedin, RAMP1, and membrane protein oxidation, (iii) attenuation of increased width, (iv) normalization of skeletal alpha-actin expression, and (v) normalization of augmented brain natriu- retic peptide expression.

oxidative stress contributes to cardiomyocyte dysfunction, hypertrophy and hypertrophic remodeling, but the mechanisms by which oxidative stress induces these processes are complex, multifactorial and incompletely understood.
oxidative stress contributes directly to induction of IMD and its receptor component RAMP1 and indirectly to induction of prepro-endothenin-1, skeletal-α actin, and BNP.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the antioxidant intervention was able to normalize the oxidative stress and the hypertrophy, but not the blood pressure in L-NAME rats.

chronic NO deficiency in cardiomyocytes induces oxidative stress and hypertrophy, which are both prevented by an antioxidant intervention, but that the latter does not affect expression of preproAM, preproIMD or RAMP2 and 3, indicating that the regulation of these genes is not dependent on oxidative stress.

chronic NO deficiency is associated with augmented oxidative stress, hypertrophy and increased expression of prepro AM and prepro-IM, and their receptor components, RAMP1, RAMP2, RAMP3, and that these changes are prevented by blood pressure reduction and/or by antioxidant intervention.
The main takeaway from our work is that

oxidative stress is a key factor contributing to the development of cardiac hypertrophy in NO deficiency and that the effects of antioxidant interventions on cardiomyocyte hypertrophic remodeling are not necessarily related to blood pressure lowering.
the cardiomyocyte IMD-RAMP1 signaling cascade is a potential therapeutic target to prevent hypertrophy and fibrosis in NO-deficient myocardium.
the expression of IMD/RAMP1 is regulated by a distinct mechanism that is not dependent upon blood pressure and is not secondary to cardiomyocytic hypertrophy.
